# The D5 Model {#sec-d5}

Software systems have a problem of containers. Where does *this* piece of code belong? Which folder, which module, which service, which team, which release cadence? The classical answer (*organise by layer: controllers here, services there, repositories below*) fails because layers are not containers of meaning. A layer is a slice of mechanism. The question "where does the registration logic live?" has the same answer as "where does the payments logic live?" under a layered scheme: *all over the place*.

The Codex's answer is the **D5 model**: five nested containers, organised by meaning, every one of them named for what it *is*, not for the mechanism it uses.

## The five levels

```
Domain
└── Division
    └── Department
        └── Desk
              ⇣ ⇡
            Dossier flows through Desks
```

Each level contains the level below. The Dossier is unusual: it is not a container but the *artifact that flows through* containers. We will say more about that in a moment.

| Level | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Domain** | The whole problem space the organisation serves | "Library Services" |
| **Division** | A cohesive piece of software with its own release cycle and bounded vocabulary | "Lending" |
| **Department** | One of three departments inside a Division (CMD, PRJ, QRY) | the *Lending CMD* |
| **Desk** | A single capability; one verb, one subject | *register_book*, *issue_loan* |
| **Dossier** | The artifact that accumulates events as it passes through Desks | *Loan #018f6a7b* |

That is the whole model. The rest of this chapter is what each level *means*, what each one is *not*, and how they compose.

## Domain; the whole problem space

A Domain is what the organisation is *for*. "Library Services" is a Domain. "Payments". "Logistics". "Insurance Underwriting". A Domain has many Divisions but only one identity.

The senior usage in Eric Evans's *Domain-Driven Design* uses "domain" exactly this way: the entire problem space. The Codex uses it the same way. A common-room confusion in DDD discourse is the *other* usage; *domain* as a near-synonym for *bounded context*. This Codex calls a bounded context a **Division**. The reasons are mechanical: Domains do not have release cycles, do not have technology stacks, do not deploy. Divisions do all three. Conflating them blurs which thing is being argued about.

A Domain rarely shows up in a codebase. It shows up on a strategy slide, in a leadership conversation, in a name above the engineering org-chart. When a Domain appears in the system at all, it is as a top-level repo-group or workspace name. Below that line, the Domain dissolves into Divisions.

## Division; a cohesive piece of software

A Division is one bounded context, one cohesive software system, one release cycle, one technology stack. It has the property a Domain lacks: you can deploy it.

A Division is the unit of *team ownership* and *autonomous release*. The Lending team owns the Lending Division; they release on their own cadence; they choose their own runtime. The Lending Division has a vocabulary (*Loan*, *Borrower*, *Reservation*) that is locally consistent and may differ from other Divisions. The library may have a separate *Acquisitions Division* with its own vocabulary (*Order*, *Vendor*, *Receipt*) that overlaps in places but does not need to agree everywhere.

Two Divisions communicate via well-defined integration points (events on a shared bus, or RPC across the gateway) never via shared databases. The integration points are slow and explicit. Inside a Division, the vocabulary is fast and intimate.

The classical bounded-context literature underdeveloped this distinction by reusing "domain" for the thing we call Division. The Codex insists on the rename because the same word for the strategy-slide concept and the deployable concept makes every architecture conversation harder.

## Department; CMD, PRJ, QRY

Inside a Division there are always exactly three Departments. They are not optional and they are not negotiable.

- **CMD**; the *command* side. Receives commands, validates them against state, emits events.
- **PRJ**; the *projection* side. Subscribes to events, builds read models, materialises views.
- **QRY**; the *query* side. Serves reads from the read models built by PRJ.

This is straightforward CQRS, with one structural commitment the literature usually leaves implicit: **CMD, PRJ, and QRY are sibling deployables, not layers of the same deployable**. They can be in the same OS process or in three; either way they are not stacked. The arrow from CMD to PRJ is an event subscription, not a function call. The arrow from PRJ to QRY is a read-model handoff, not an inheritance relation.

The Department names (CMD, PRJ, QRY) are deliberately three letters and deliberately not English words. They appear in folder names, repo names, app names. *manage_loans/* is a CMD; *query_loans/* is a QRY. The third Department, PRJ, is usually fused into the QRY app (the projections are *for* the queries) but is logically distinct.

## Desk; a single capability

A Desk is one verb, one subject, one outcome. *register_book*, *issue_loan*, *return_loan*, *renew_loan*, *flag_overdue*. Each Desk is one capability that the Division offers; to its users, to other Divisions, to time itself in the case of scheduled work.

A Desk lives in one folder. The folder name *screams* what the Desk does, because the convention is: folders are verb_subject. Inside the folder, all the code for that capability lives together; the command record, the event record, the handler, the projection that depends on its events. This is *vertical slicing* and Chapter 3 has the full treatment. For now: a Desk is a slice.

Desks belong to Departments. A CMD Department has Desks like *issue_loan/*. A QRY Department has Desks like *get_loan_by_id/* or *list_overdue_loans_page/*. The naming convention shifts subtly between CMD and QRY: CMD Desks use a present-tense business verb; QRY Desks use *get_* / *list_* / *count_* + a noun.

A Division might have thirty Desks. Forty. More. Listing them in their folder gives a reader the complete capability inventory of the Division in one glance; no class diagrams, no architecture slides, no documentation. *That is the point of a Desk being a folder*.

## Dossier; the artifact that flows through Desks

The first four levels are containers. The fifth is different: a **Dossier** is what *passes through* the containers, accumulating events as it goes.

In the lending library, a *Loan* is a Dossier. It begins life when a Borrower issues a *issue_loan* command at the *issue_loan* Desk: an event lands, *loan_opened_v1*. It continues when the Borrower renews: another event, *loan_renewed_v1*. It concludes when the book is returned: *loan_returned_v1*. It is archived when retention windows expire: *loan_archived_v1*. The Dossier is the entire stream of those events, in order. It has an identity (a stream ID), a lifetime (initiate → conclude → archive), and a history (the events).

A Dossier is not a database row. A Dossier *is* its history. Rebuilding state means replaying the events front to back. The "current state" of a Dossier is a derived quantity, computed by folding the events. There is no canonical *Loan* table in the canonical sense; there is a stream of Loan events, and there are projections that materialise convenient views of those streams into tables.

Validation in this world becomes: *can this slip be added to this Dossier?*; where a slip is one new event we are proposing to append. *Can a loan_renewed_v1 be added to this Loan? Only if the Loan is currently opened, not returned, not archived.* The Dossier's history tells us, deterministically, what its current state is, and therefore which slips can or cannot be added.

The word *Dossier* is chosen carefully. It evokes a paper folder that accumulates documents over time. A Dossier is not a database record or a state field; it is a folder of paper, and you read it front to back to know what happened.

Some Dossiers live briefly (a Loan exists for a few weeks); others span years (a Membership); some never close (a Catalogue Entry might be revised but never archived). Whatever the lifetime, the rule is *one Dossier per instance*: one Loan, one Membership, one Catalogue Entry. The stream IDs are the instance identities.

## Why this and not the classical layers

The classical layered architecture organises by mechanism: controllers, services, repositories, models. The D5 model organises by meaning: a Domain has Divisions; a Division has Departments; a Department has Desks; Desks process Dossiers.

The trade is real and worth naming. Layered architectures are easier to *staff* (you can hire a "service-layer developer") and easier to *standardise* (every service looks like every other service). D5 architectures are easier to *navigate* (the folder names tell you what the system does) and easier to *change* (changes to one capability stay in one folder).

The Codex chooses navigation and changeability over staffing and standardisation, for one reason: when systems live for years, the navigation-and-change costs dominate. The staffing-and-standardisation costs are upfront. Software that pays its costs at the start and reaps benefits over time is software that ages well.

## What this enables

The rest of the book leans heavily on the D5 vocabulary. Chapter 3 will explain why a Division is shaped like a pizza, not an onion. Chapter 4 will explain why every Desk folder is named so it screams. Chapter 5 will explain how a Dossier's concurrency is enforced (and when you need a Decision instead). Chapter 7 will explain how Divisions are built (the *Reckon Cycle*) from inception through rescue. Part II will show you the actual code that makes the levels real.

If you remember nothing else from this chapter, remember this: the system has five levels, and the bottom one (the Dossier) flows through the other four, accumulating events. Everything else in the book is consequence.
